Appendix C Instructions for Experiments 3 and 4

The instructions for each condition in Experiments 3 and 4 consisted of three paragraphs, each of which was from the following subsections according to the combination of the independent variables. For instance, the instruction for the two-outcome-control-prediction-one-off condition is as follows:

Three cards have the number 0, and the other three have the number 5. The number displayed on the card has no relation to the points.

On the next page, you will be asked to write down which card will be drawn if the game is played once.

After you complete the task, the program will play the game once for real. Please be aware that your answer will not influence the result.

Two-outcome-control:

Three cards have the number 0, and the other three have the number 5. The number displayed on the card has no relation to the points.

Two-outcome-gain:

Three cards have outcome +0, and the other three have outcome +5. The outcome displayed on the card will determine the number of points you earn. For example, drawing the card with "+0" results in winning 0 points, while drawing the card with "+5" results in winning 5 points.

Two-outcome-loss:

Three cards have outcome -0, and the other three have outcome -5. The outcome displayed on the card will determine the number of points you lose. For example, drawing the card with "-0" results in losing 0 points, while drawing the card with "-5" results in losing 5 points.

Six-outcome-control:

Each card is printed with the numbers 0 to 5. The number displayed on the card has no relation to the points.

Six-Outcome-Gain:

Each card is printed with the outcomes +0 to +5. The outcome displayed on the card will determine the number of points you earn. For example, drawing the card with "+0" results in winning 0 points, while drawing the card with "+5" Repeated-gain: After you complete the task, the program will play the game ten times for real, and the results will be added to the points you win. Please be aware that your answer will not influence the results.

Repeated-loss:

After you complete the task, the program will play the game ten times for real, and the results will be added to the points you lose. Please be aware that your answer will not influence the results.

Appendix D Determinism

In this section, we explain the definition of determinism (DET) and the reason for setting 1511 90% as one of our exclusion criteria. This measure was developed by Marwan et al. (2007) 1512 to analyse recurrence in a sequence. A high DET indicates that a large proportion of 1513 recurrent responses form repeated sequences, reflecting greater predictability in the 1514 generated outcomes. We used this measure to identify highly repetitive response patterns 1515 that may depart from the intended random generation task.

1516

The measure is based on the recurrence plot, which shows whether the element x i in 1517 a sequence is the same as x j . Figure D1 shows an example of the recurrence plot for the 1518 sequence {4, 2, 1, 5, 4, 3, 2, 5, 4, 1}.

1519

DET measures the percentage of the dots on the plot that fall on diagonal lines with length equal to or larger than 2: where l is the length of a diagonal, and C(l) is the count of the diagonal with length l.

For example, in Figure D1, there are eight diagonals of length 1 (single dots), two diagonals of length 2, and one diagonal of length 10 (the main diagonal). The DET for the example sequence is:

Appendix G Analysis of Experiment 4 Following the Preregistration

In this section, we present the analysis of Experiment 4 following the originally planned exclusion criteria. The results below are for the final sample of 15 participants. The analysis outline remained identical to Experiments 3 and 4.

Group-level Analysis

First we compared the averaged histogram of the numbers in each domain and each level of the number of outcomes with the theoretical uniform distributions. As shown in Figure G1, we observed the same optimistic pattern that we found in Experiments 3 and 4.

Next, we examined the mean values for each of the 24 conditions, comparing them with the theoretical mean of 2.5. Conditions with mean values significantly different from 2.5 were identified after applying a Holm-Bonferroni correction. As illustrated in Figure G2, the domain effects were consistent: mean values in the gain domain were higher than 2.5, while those in the loss domain were lower than 2.5.

An RM-BANOVA was used to analyse the influence of all the independent variables and their interactions, and Table G1 presents the corresponding BF. In Experiment 4, the BF for repetition provided very strong evidence against an effect. In contrast, the BF for the domains decisively supported the presence of an influence. The BFs for both the tasks and the interaction between domain and task were lower than 1/3, providing strong and substantial evidence against the effects, respectively.

We also considered the possibility of an ineffective manipulation since the task instruction did not affect responses. We analysed only the first block using a one-way Bayesian ANOVA to test the effect of the task and the BF was 1/5.02, again indicating substantial evidence for the absence of a task effect.

Individual-level Analysis

Appendix H The Starting Point

This section reports analyses focusing on the starting point of mental simulation, defined as the initial value in the sampling sequence. First, we examined an additional bias observed in the data: in several experiments, participants showed systematic tendencies in the values chosen as their first response, which we refer to as the starting-point bias. Second, in Experiments 3 and 4, we tested whether the value provided in the one-off condition could be regarded as the starting point of the repeated condition. These analyses were not central to our main research question and are presented as exploratory. They should therefore be interpreted with caution and examined more systematically in future work.

Experiment 1

In Experiment 1, we conducted an RM-BANOVA considering the domains, the starting points (whether the number is the first one or not) and their interaction as the fixed effects. We also accounted for the random effect of subjects. The BFs were 1/3.02, 2.80 × 10 3 and 1/9.37 for the domains, starting point and their interaction, respectively. As indicated in these BFs, participants exhibited a starting-point bias. Figure H1 shows that participants typically began with a relatively small value, and all subsequent numbers were distributed more evenly.

Experiment 2

In Experiment 2, we ran the same RM-BANOVA including domain, starting point, and their interaction. The BF for the domain was 1/9.83, again providing substantial evidence against a utility effect at the group level. By contrast, the BF for the starting point was 1/2.61, offering no evidence of a bias, and the BF for the interaction was 1/38.86, indicating very strong evidence against an interaction between domain and starting point.

We propose that the absence of the starting-point bias observed in Experiment 2 is due to participants' tendency to begin with the most probable outcome when the distribution is non-uniform. The binomial distribution, in particular, is a special case the repeated condition, and the subsequent numbers in the repeated condition. experimental program. Future studies could address this concern by conducting in-person experiments in which gambles are resolved visibly in front of participants as we did in Experiments 1 and 2, ensuring full transparency of the outcome mechanism. A fourth consideration concerns the large differences in DET between Experiments 3 and 4: Experiment 4 has more participants with high DET than Experiment 3. As shown by Figure D2(B), this difference was particularly apparent near the upper boundary of the distribution (98-100%). Such high values can arise from highly predictable response patterns (see Appendix D for examples). These patterns may reflect simplified response strategies, such as exclusively selecting one outcome or following a predetermined response cycle, rather than independently imagining each draw. Such strategies may arise from different approaches to the task, including attempts to reproduce expected outcome frequencies or reduce cognitive effort, although the present data cannot establish their underlying causes.
